script_claims.note: Checks requested by the manager for War/SCRIPT.md:654 (sources/SCRIPT.md:597). R16 is the register entry for these figures; it is not an assigned gate of XTRA-20, so it is not closed here. War/SCRIPT.md was not edited.

claims.claim: Users needed the VB runtime, a DLL that shipped separately from the program.
evidence: source/original.txt lines 591-592: VBRUN.ZIP 169469 06-09-92 "The Dynamic Link Library required to run any compiled Visual Basic program." (listed as its own download in Main Board Directory 04 - Games!)

http://www.textfiles.com/bbs/FILELISTS/southexp.lst (Southern Express BBS, 1992; SHA-256 1fa6815b283cdeb89761f312466bced90ed34ebfb2dfdd7de082ec52a310be91) lines 3410-3412: VBRUN100.ZIP 169480 06-23-91 "Microsoft's visual basic runtime. Download this and save the trouble of including it in all uploads and downloads in V.B. programs"
Microsoft KB Q99251 (https://jeffpar.github.io/kbarchive/kb/099/Q99251/): VBRUN300.DLL distributed as the self-extracting VBRUN300.EXE; VBRUN100.DLL and VBRUN200.DLL as VBRUN100.EXE and VBRUN200.EXE.
claims.result: The listing shows the runtime as a separate board download. The Southern Express entry also shows that authors bundled it into uploads and that boards encouraged a separate copy instead.

claims.claim: The DLL was called something like VBRUN300.DLL.
evidence: Microsoft KB Q99251: VBRUN300.DLL is the Visual Basic 3.0 runtime; fixed build 03.00.0538, 12-MAY-1993, 398416 bytes (earlier 03.00.0537, 04-APR-1993, 394384 bytes).
Microsoft KB Q196286 (https://jeffpar.github.io/kbarchive/kb/196/Q196286/): Visual Basic 4.0 apps use Vb40016.dll (913KB) or Vb40032.dll (705KB).
The XTRA-20 listing (1992) shows VBRUN.ZIP with no version; it does not show VBRUN300. No textfiles.com FILELISTS listing (1989-1994) mentions VBRUN300.
claims.result: VBRUN300.DLL is a real, correctly named VB3 runtime. The narration hedges with "something like", which matters because the story is VB4-era, and VB4's runtimes were VB40016.DLL/VB40032.DLL. The frame must not be captioned as showing VBRUN300.

claims.claim: Bundling the runtime turned a 200-kilobyte game into a 1.5-megabyte download.
evidence: Microsoft KB Q99251: VBRUN300.DLL is 398416 bytes uncompressed.
Internet Archive item VBRUN300_ZIP (https://archive.org/metadata/VBRUN300_ZIP): VBRUN300.ZIP is 228521 bytes. Uploader-supplied item; used only as an order-of-magnitude compressed size.
This listing: VBRUN.ZIP (pre-VB3 runtime) is 169469 bytes.
claims.calculation: 200,000 + 398,416 = 598,416 bytes uncompressed (about 0.6 MB); 200,000 + 228,521 = 428,521 bytes with the zipped runtime (about 0.43 MB). Reaching 1.5 MB needs roughly 0.9-1.1 MB more, such as extra VBX controls or the VB4 16-bit runtime (Vb40016.dll 913KB per KB Q196286).
claims.result: The VB3 runtime alone gives about 0.4-0.6 MB, not 1.5 MB. Review question for the Writing Lead.

claims.claim: On a 14.4 modem, 1.5 MB is nearly ten minutes of downloading.
evidence: ITU-T Recommendation V.32 bis (02/1991), https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-V.32bis: duplex modem at data signalling rates of up to 14 400 bit/s.
claims.calculation: Upper bound 14,400 / 8 = 1,800 bytes/s (error-corrected link with no start/stop bits); 14,400 / 10 = 1,440 bytes/s for plain asynchronous 8N1 framing. An already-zipped download gains nothing from modem compression. 1,500,000 bytes takes 833 s (13.9 min) to 1,042 s (17.4 min). Ten minutes corresponds to 864,000-1,080,000 bytes. 598,416 bytes takes 5.5-6.9 min; 428,521 bytes takes 4.0-5.0 min.
claims.result: "Nearly ten minutes" understates 1.5 MB at 14.4k by about 40% or more. These are arithmetic from the nominal line rate, not measured transfers. The same 14.4k ≈ 9+ minute figure appears in the progress-bar mockup at War/SCRIPT.md:854. Review question for the Writing Lead.

review_questions.question: War/SCRIPT.md:654 figures do not reconcile: the VB3 runtime makes a 200 KB game about 0.4-0.6 MB, not 1.5 MB, and 1.5 MB at 14.4k is about 14-17 minutes, not nearly ten. Proposed fix (option A, keeps VBRUN300): "...which could turn a 200-kilobyte game into a download two or three times that size. On a 14.4 modem, that's another four or five minutes of waiting. For a card game." Option B (keeps the big numbers, VB4 16-bit runtime): "...which could turn a 200-kilobyte game into a download of more than a megabyte. On a 14.4 modem, that's over ten minutes of downloading. For a card game." Keep the progress-bar mockup at line 854 consistent with whichever is chosen.
